seo.title: Horizontal Tank Liquid Volume Calculator
seo.description: Partially Filled Horizontal Tank Volume Calculator — Calculate liquid volume in a partially-filled horizontal cylindrical tank from fill level with instant results & multiple unit support.

formula.explanation: Liquid volume = Cross-sectional area × Length. Cross-section = r²·arccos((r−h)/r) − (r−h)·√(2rh−h²) (circular segment formula). ×1000 converts m³ to liters. Where r = radius, h = fill height.

inputs.label: Liquid Fill Height
inputs.hint: From tank bottom, not exceeding diameter

content.introduction: Calculate the liquid volume in a partially filled horizontal cylinder using the circular segment area formula. This is the standard method for dipstick-to-volume conversion for horizontal fuel tanks, water trucks, and bulk storage.

example.description: 3m diameter × 6m horizontal tank filled to 1m height holds ~12,395 liters (out of 42,412 total at 100%).

faq.a: This gives a theoretical result for a perfect cylindrical shell with flat ends. Real tanks with dished heads or internal baffles require a strapping table calibration.

At h = r (half full), the volume is exactly half the total volume. Due to the circular geometry, fill height is not linear with volume: at 30% height you have ~25% volume, at 50% height you have exactly 50% volume.

faq.q: How do I calculate the total (100%) tank volume?
faq.a: Total volume = pi x r^2 x L. For a 3 m diameter x 6 m tank: 3.1416 x 1.5^2 x 6 = 42.41 m3 = 42,412 L. The calculator's result at h = 2r (full) equals this value.

faq.q: Why is fill height not linear with volume?
faq.a: The cross-section is a circle, so the wetted area grows slowly near the bottom and top and fastest at mid-height. At 25% height you have only ~19.5% volume; at 75% height you already have ~80.5%. Always use the segment formula or a dipstick chart.

faq.q: How do I convert liters to gallons?
faq.a: 1 US gallon = 3.785 L; 1 imperial gallon = 4.546 L. Example: 7,370 L = 7,370 / 3.785 = 1,947 US gallons = 1,621 imperial gallons.

faq.q: How accurate is this for tanks with dished heads?
faq.a: The formula covers only the straight cylindrical shell. Dished or elliptical heads add 5-15% volume depending on head type and depth. For custody-transfer accuracy, calibrate with a strapping table or use the head-volume correction.

sections.heading: Horizontal Tank Volume Formula Explained
sections.body:
The liquid volume in a partially filled horizontal cylinder is the circular segment area times the shell length:

V = [r^2 x acos((r - h)/r) - (r - h) x sqrt(2 x r x h - h^2)] x L

Where r = tank radius (m), h = liquid fill height (m), L = straight shell length (m). The result is in m3; multiply by 1000 for liters.

Example: a 3 m diameter (r = 1.5 m) x 6 m tank filled to h = 1 m: segment area = 1.5^2 x acos(0.5/1.5) - 0.5 x sqrt(2 x 1.5 x 1 - 1) = 1.228 m2, volume = 1.228 x 6 = 7.37 m3 = 7,370 L.

sections.heading: Fill Height vs Volume Reference
sections.body:
For a horizontal cylinder, volume is NOT linear with fill height:

| Fill Height (h/r) | % of Total Volume |
|---|---|
| 10% | 5.2% |
| 25% | 19.5% |
| 50% (h = r) | 50.0% |
| 75% | 80.5% |
| 90% | 94.8% |

At 30% height you have only ~25% volume; at 70% height you already have ~75%. This nonlinearity is why dipstick charts are needed for accurate inventory — a linear gauge would be wrong by up to 10% of tank volume.

sections.heading: Worked Example: Dipstick Calibration
sections.body:
A 3 m diameter x 6 m horizontal tank (total capacity 42,412 L) needs a dipstick chart. At h = 1 m:

V = 7.37 m3 = 7,370 L (17.4% of capacity)

At h = 1.5 m (half full): V = 21,206 L (exactly 50%). At h = 2.5 m: V = 35,042 L (82.6%). Generate a table at 0.1 m increments for the operator's dipstick. For tanks with dished heads, add the head volume and calibrate against a strapping table.
